where: Section 1, last line on Carmichael value
problem: The conclusion is right but the reason given is backwards. 'Any d with e·d ≡ 1 (mod λ(n)) also decrypts, because λ(n) divides φ(n)' does not follow: λ | φ only shows that a d which is an inverse mod φ is also an inverse mod λ (the opposite direction). A student copying this reason learns wrong logic.
fix: Say the correct reason: λ(n) = lcm(p−1, q−1) is a multiple of both p−1 and q−1, so when e·d − 1 is a multiple of λ(n) it is a multiple of p−1 and of q−1; Fermat's little theorem then gives m^(e·d) ≡ m modulo p and modulo q, hence modulo n. Using λ(n) only enlarges the set of valid d compared with φ(n).

problem: The arrow leaving the node labelled 'Private d' and entering 'Public key (e, n)' is labelled 'publish'. Read literally that says d is published, which is exactly the secret.
fix: Label that edge something like 'form public key' or attach the 'publish' label to the node (e, n) itself, so the only published values are e and n.

problem: 'Notice that n alone is published while its two prime factors are destroyed' conflicts with the public pair (e, n) stated everywhere else in the chapter; it reads as if e is secret.
fix: 'Notice that n and e are published while p, q and φ(n) are destroyed.'

problem: d = 27 is correct mod φ(n) = 40, but it is not the smallest working exponent for this key: λ(n) = lcm(4, 10) = 20, so d = 7 also decrypts (14⁷ mod 55 = 9). Students meet the trap 'every d ≡ e⁻¹ mod λ(n) decrypts' just below and may think something is wrong.
fix: Add one line: here λ(n) = lcm(4, 10) = 20, so d = 7 works as well as 27; the example keeps 27 because it was computed mod φ(n).

problem: 'An attacker holds n, e and c and wants d' misstates the goal (the attacker wants m), and 'no method better than factoring is known' is stated too strongly: recovering d from (e, n) is as hard as factoring, but breaking RSA by recovering m is not proven to be equivalent to factoring.
fix: 'An attacker holds n, e and c and wants m. The best known attacks need the factorisation of n, and recovering d from (e, n) is provably as hard as factoring; no attack on RSA itself is known that beats factoring n.'

problem: 'constant-time code and random blinding hide them' is loose: constant-time code does not hide the bits of d, it removes any dependence of the running time on them.
fix: 'decryption time follows the bits of d, so implementations use constant-time exponentiation (no data-dependent branches) and random blinding of the ciphertext to break the link between timing and d.'
